# Abstract

The Vedic period in northern and western South Asia represents one of the most decisive socioeconomic transformations in Old World protohistory, spanning the structural transition from the decentralised post-urban Indus agropastoral landscape to the fortified urban polities of the Gangetic plain on the eve of the Second Urbanisation. Encompassing 2.013.529 km² (2,01M km²) across four physiographic macro-regions and 26.445 active terrestrial grid cells, the subcontinent witnessed profound ecological reorganisation following mid-second-millennium aridification and the progressive hydrographic decline of the Ghaggar-Hakra drainage system. As agropastoral populations expanded eastward from the Sapta Sindhu and the Punjab plains across the Kurukshetra divide into the lush, rainfed monsoon alluvium of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and the Middle Ganga basin, new technological and metallurgical regimes reconfigured carrying capacity. The introduction of iron smelting and wrought implements from 1200BC to 1000BC, coupled with the systematic adoption of double-cropping regimes uniting winter wheat and barley with summer wet-paddy rice cultivation, provided the energetic basis for sustained demographic acceleration. Between 1500BC and 500BC, the regional population more than tripled, rising from 5,2M to 18,5M inhabitants and driving aggregate demographic density from 258,25 to 918,78 persons per 100 km². Growth was concentrated in the Painted Grey Ware core of Kurukshetra, Panchala and the Upper Doab (expanding from 1,77M to 6,29M inhabitants) and the fertile alluvial corridors of Kosala, Videha and early Magadha (climbing from 1,25M to 4,44M inhabitants), while the western semi-arid peripheries of Rajasthan, Malwa and Gujarat sustained steady agropastoral settlement [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. This study integrates 5.905 catalogued settlement trajectories georeferenced to WGS84 coordinates (conforming to a Zipf rank-size distribution with $\alpha = 0,85$, $R^2 = 0,97$) with 26.445 five-arcminute raster cells and a source ledger of 6.705 evaluated candidate localities, establishing an archaeological demographic foundation for Iron Age South Asia.

# Background

## Environmental Transition and Riverine Reorganisation

The transition from the Mature Harappan urban network to the Early Vedic agropastoral horizon unfolded against a backdrop of macro-climatic instability across western South Asia [@Kumari2025Late; @Dimri2022Monsoon]. During the second millennium BC, the weakening of the southwest summer monsoon altered the hydrographic equilibrium of the Indus-Punjab drainage basin and adjacent channels [@Neogi2019Geoarchaeo]. Most significantly, the palaeo-channel of the Ghaggar-Hakra, celebrated in the early hymns of the Rigveda as the Sarasvati, suffered progressive discharge reduction, siltation and headwater capture by neighbouring drainage networks [@Oldham1932Indian; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. 

While Mature Harappan settlement patterns had relied upon seasonal flood-recession inundation agriculture along semi-arid river margins in Sindh, Cholistan and the Punjab, the reduction in perennial glacial meltwater and monsoon run-off rendered large nucleated civic centres unsustainable [@Anon1994; @Dhurandhar2025Genomic]. Populations adapted not through demographic collapse, but through spatial decentralisation and eastward dispersal into higher-rainfall ecological zones. The sub-Himalayan foothill corridors, the Siwalik piedmonts and the moist alluvium of the Upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab offered predictable precipitation exceeding 700 mm annually, enabling rainfed cultivation and diverse pastoral subsistence regimes [@Joshi2026Socio; @Rakesh2022Ecological]. 

Geoarchaeological coring throughout northwest India indicates that by 1500BC, sedentary hamlets were colonising river terraces along the Yamuna, Hindon, Kali and upper Ganga, establishing the settlement substrate from which the Vedic cultural complex emerged [@Neogi2019Geoarchaeo; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Floodplain sedimentation patterns in the Doab reveal active levee formation that provided well-drained residential perimeters directly flanking nutrient-rich backswamps.

## The Four Macro-Regions of the Vedic Sphere

The demographic modelling framework partitions the 2,01M km² domain of Northern and Western South Asia into four physiographically and ecologically coherent macro-regions:

1. Sapta Sindhu, Gandhara and Indus-Punjab Plains (444.682 km², 22,08% of regional area; 1.391 catalogued settlements): Spanning the five rivers of the Punjab (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej), the upper Indus trunk, the Potwar plateau and the Vale of Peshawar in Gandhara. This region forms the primary stage of early Vedic pastoral mobility and Gandhara Grave culture interaction [@Olivieri2022Stoneyards; @Jassar2009Hellas; @Possehl1999IndusAge].
2. Kurukshetra, Upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab and Panchala (335.615 km², 16,67% of regional area; 1.317 catalogued settlements): The primary heartland of Later Vedic lineage formation and the Painted Grey Ware ceramic horizon, extending from the Ghaggar basin across Kurukshetra and the interfluve of the Yamuna and Ganga to the borders of eastern Uttar Pradesh [@Latief2026Tibba; @Thapar1981Indian; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation].
3. Middle Ganga, Kosala, Videha and Early Magadha (258.210 km², 12,82% of regional area; 1.501 catalogued settlements): The humid subtropical alluvium of the middle Gangetic plains, characterised by dense aquatic networks, oxbow lakes, extensive rice paddy ecology and the emergence of the Black and Red Ware to pre-NBPW urban predecessors [@Kumar2023Second; @Sengupta2023Fish; @Allchin1995Archaeology].
4. Malwa, Matsya, Rajasthan and Western Chalcolithic Periphery (975.022 km², 48,42% of regional area; 1.696 catalogued settlements): An expansive ecological frontier encompassing the Aravalli range, the semi-arid Thar desert margins, the fertile black cotton soils of the Malwa plateau and the maritime estuaries of Gujarat, maintaining regional continuity from the post-Harappan Ahar-Banas and Malwa Chalcolithic traditions [@Schug2009Ancient; @Mishra2026Historical; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].

The structural boundaries between these four divisions correspond to prominent geomorphic features: the Delhi ridge acts as the physical threshold between the Indus and Ganga drainage basins, while the Rajmahal hills in the east mark the entrance to the humid deltaic plains of Bengal, and the Aravalli chain separates the semi-arid Thar from the arable Malwa tableland.

## Archaeoceramic Sequences: From OCP and Cemetery H to PGW and NBPW

The material culture of the Vedic era is defined by a succession of regional ceramic traditions that trace the shifting geographical focus of sedentary populations [@Malapaka2025Archaeocer; @Latief2026Tibba]. Following the dissolution of Mature Harappan urban uniformity around 1900BC to 1700BC, northwest South Asia fragmented into distinctive regional assemblages: the Cemetery H culture in the central Punjab, the Jhukar style in Sindh, the Gandhara Grave culture across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) tradition along the upper Doab and eastern Rajasthan [@Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities; @Olivieri2022Stoneyards]. The OCP horizon, frequently associated with copper hoards containing anthropomorphic figures, harpoons and celts, occupied river bluffs subject to periodic sheet-flooding, sustaining semi-permanent agrarian hamlets between 2000BC and 1500BC [@Thapar1981Indian].

By the late second millennium BC, the emergence of Black and Red Ware (BRW) and Painted Grey Ware (PGW) marked a definitive technological and structural transformation [@Malapaka2025Archaeocer]. Painted Grey Ware, produced from well-levigated alluvial clays fired in reduction kilns to produce an even grey surface adorned with black geometric designs, became the diagnostic ceramic horizon of the Kuru-Panchala heartland [@Latief2026Tibba; @Thapar1981Indian]. Stratigraphic sequences at key excavations including Hastinapur, Atranjikhera, Noh, Bhagwanpura and Jakhera reveal continuous occupation sequences where PGW deposits overlie Late Harappan or OCP layers without occupational hiatus [@Thapar1981Indian]. At Bhagwanpura in Haryana, Joshi documented the direct interstratification of Late Harappan and PGW ceramics, confirming cultural continuity and technological exchange during the middle of the second millennium BC.

In the Middle Ganga basin, the ceramic trajectory followed an autonomous yet interconnected development anchored by early Black and Red Ware (BRW) assemblages [@Kumar2023Second; @Malapaka2025Archaeocer]. At sites such as Sohgaura, Chirand, Narhan and Taradih, early BRW horizons precede the arrival of NBPW, associated with bone tools, microliths and early copper implements. Towards the end of the first millennium BC, the PGW tradition transitioned into the lustrous Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), reflecting pyrotechnological refinement, expanding exchange networks and the administrative nucleation of the early historic Mahajanapadas [@Kumar2023Second].

## Agrarian Economy: Iron Metallurgy, Double-Cropping and Cattle Pastoralism

The expansion of population across the heavily forested Gangetic alluvium required substantial metallurgical and agronomic developments [@Rakesh2022Ecological; @Kumar2023Second]. The indigenous emergence of iron technology around 1200BC to 1000BC, attested at Atranjikhera, Noh, Kaushambi and Raja Nal Ka Tila, transformed agricultural clearance [@Thapar1981Indian; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Kumar2023Second]. While copper and bronze tools were inadequate for clearing dense subtropical hardwood canopies dominated by sal (*Shorea robusta*) and teak, heavy socketed iron axes and iron-tipped ard-points enabled systematic deforestation and the cultivation of thick, moisture-retentive alluvial soils [@Rakesh2022Ecological].

Concurrently, archaeobotanical recovery demonstrates the establishment of an intensive double-cropping (rabi and kharif) agricultural cycle [@Saraswat1991Archaeobot; @Biswas2024Environmen]. Winter crops inherited from the western Asian agricultural package (wheat *Triticum aestivum*, barley *Hordeum vulgare*, peas and lentils) were systematically combined with indigenous summer monsoon staples, principally wet-paddy rice (*Oryza sativa*), pearl millet (*Pennisetum glaucum*), sorghum and pulses [@Saraswat1991Archaeobot]. Archaeobotanical flotation records from Atranjikhera and Narhan document the systematic exploitation of pulse cultivars, including green gram (*Vigna radiata*), black gram (*Vigna mungo*) and horsegram (*Macrotyloma uniflorum*), alongside oilseeds such as sesame (*Sesamum indicum*) and mustard (*Brassica* sp.) [@Saraswat1991Archaeobot]. Rice cultivation in the swampy backwaters of the Ganga and Yamuna generated caloric yields far exceeding dry cereal farming, creating the grain surpluses necessary to support non-agricultural craft specialists, sacerdotal lineages and territorial administrators.

Alongside crop agriculture, cattle pastoralism remained the structural anchor of Vedic society [@Dwivedi2019Indic; @Donder2025Spiritual]. Faunal assemblages across PGW horizons at Hastinapur, Atranjikhera and Rupnagar are heavily dominated by domesticated zebu cattle (*Bos indicus*), alongside water buffalo (*Bubalus bubalis*), sheep, goat and pig [@Thapar1981Indian]. Cattle served multiple economic functions: providing draught power for tillage and cart transport, producing milk and clarified butter (*ghee*) for dietary sustenance and sacrificial rituals, supplying manure for soil replenishment and functioning as the primary measure of movable wealth (*rayi*) and social status [@Dwivedi2019Indic; @Pokharel2026Revisiting].

## Riverine Transport and the Uttarapatha Corridor

Water transport provided the primary physical integration across the vast distances of the Gangetic plain [@Mishra2026Historical; @Kulke2009Bibliograp]. The perennial trunk streams of the Ganga and Yamuna, fed by Himalayan glaciers and supplemented by tributaries such as the Chambal, Betwa, Ghaghara, Gomti and Gandak, offered navigable waterways that allowed heavy freight to move downstream with minimal energetic cost. Flat-bottomed timber barges and dugout craft transported grain surpluses, building timber from Himalayan forests, copper ingots from Rajasthan and iron blooms from eastern Chota Nagpur.

Complementing this riverine transport, the great northern overland route (the proto-Uttarapatha) developed along the piedmont and Doab terraces, connecting Taxila and the Gandhara passes with Indraprastha, Mathura, Kashi and early Magadha [@Olivieri2022Stoneyards; @Kumar2023Second]. This transport corridor facilitated seasonal pastoral transhumance, trade caravans and military mobility, laying the communicative infrastructure that eventually linked the northwestern frontier directly with the Bay of Bengal.

## Social Differentiation, Lineage Systems and Janapada Formation

The political structure of the Vedic period underwent a continuous evolution from kinship-based pastoral bands (*vis* and *jana*) to territorial polities (*janapadas*) [@Dwivedi2019Indic; @Donder2025Spiritual]. In the Rigvedic phase, leadership was vested in the *rajan*, an elected or hereditary war-leader whose authority was checked by popular tribal assemblies, the *sabha* and *samiti*. Wealth was counted in cattle, horses and copper ornaments, and warfare focused on cattle raids (*gavishti*) rather than territorial conquest.

As populations became firmly rooted in sedentary agriculture during the Later Vedic period, territorial boundaries crystallised around lineage segments [@Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Mandavilli2022Introducin]. The Kuru-Panchala realm emerged as the exemplary model of Vedic statecraft, establishing administrative centres at Asandhivat, Hastinapur and Kampilya. Ritual specialists (*brahmanas*) elaborated solemn state sacrifices such as the *rajasuya* and *ashvamedha*, providing ideological legitimation for royal authority in exchange for land gifts, cattle and agricultural tribute (*bali*) [@Dwivedi2019Indic]. This ideological framework formalised the fourfold varna hierarchy, providing social stability and labour organisation that channelled rural agricultural surplus into emerging municipal centres.

Craft specialisation accompanied this political consolidation [@Kumar2023Second; @LeBlanc2013Indus]. Blacksmiths, coppersmiths, glassmakers, potters and weavers organised into early professional collectives that prefigured the historic *shreni* guilds. By the sixth century BC, proto-monetary standards emerged, transitioning from cattle units and gold necklets (*nishka*) to cast-copper tokens and early bent-bar silver punch-marked coins (*shatamana*), facilitating inter-regional commerce [@Allchin1995Archaeology].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Terrestrial Cell Accounting

To convert macro-regional demographic totals into high-resolution spatial surfaces across 2.013.529 km² of northern and western South Asia, the model employs a terrestrial grid consisting of 26.445 active five-arcminute raster cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated through environmental covariates that govern human carrying capacity and agropastoral settlement preference:

- Hydrographic Proximity: Distance-decay attenuation functions calibrated to perennial river channels, with primary weighting assigned to major river courses including the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej, Yamuna, Ganga, Ghaghara, Gandak, Chambal and Narmada.
- Alluvial Soil Fertility: Pedological suitability layers distinguishing fertile active alluvium (khadar) and older Pleistocene alluvium (bhangar) from skeletal lithosols and arid sandy soils in the Thar margin.
- Monsoon Precipitation Gradients: Isohyet intervals ranging from under 200 mm annually in western Rajasthan and Sindh to over 1.200 mm in the Middle Ganga basin, parameterising dryland versus wet-paddy cropping potential.
- Topographic Relief: Slope penalty functions that downweight rugged Himalayan escarpments, the Siwalik hills and steep tracts of the Aravalli and Vindhya ranges.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation Engine

To prevent the artificial inflation of rural population densities in zones containing large proto-urban settlements, the spatial engine executes a two-stage settlement subtraction algorithm:

1. Nucleated Urban Extraction: At each benchmark interval (1500BC, 1300BC, 1100BC, 900BC, 700BC and 500BC), the population allocated to catalogued settlements within each macro-region is aggregated. For each georeferenced settlement, population mass is assigned directly to its host coordinate grid cell, with overflow buffers applied to adjacent cells when municipal densities exceed agricultural thresholds.
2. Rural Population Allocation: The summed settlement population is subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope. The remaining rural population is distributed across non-settled cells proportional to their composite environmental suitability scores. Boundary feathering algorithms smooth density discontinuities along sub-regional borders, avoiding artificial cliffs between administrative partitions.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Recognising the inherent taphonomic and historiographical challenges in protohistoric demographic estimation, the model applies symmetric uncertainty envelopes of +/- 15% across all macro-regional and sub-regional benchmarks. In 1500BC, the baseline regional estimate of 5,2M is bounded between 4,42M and 5,98M inhabitants. By 500BC, the terminal benchmark of 18,5M is bounded between 15,73M and 21,28M. These intervals capture variance in estimated household sizes (ranging from 4,5 to 6,5 persons per domestic unit), site preservation factors and settlement nucleation ratios across shifting archaeological horizons [@Schug2009Ancient; @JANGIS2025Journal].

# Testing and Validation

## Geoarchaeological Correlation and Alluvial Taphonomy

The spatial distribution of catalogued sites has been tested against regional palaeohydrological and sedimentological reconstructions [@Neogi2019Geoarchaeo; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of river terraces and relict channel levees across Haryana, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh confirms that PGW and early historic settlements systematically occupied elevated palaeo-levees located one to three kilometres from active channels. This positioning provided immunity from destructive seasonal monsoon flooding while granting direct access to fertile, naturally irrigated backswamps for rice cultivation. The high correlation between our catalogued PGW sites and verified alluvial terraces confirms the geoarchaeological validity of the settlement database.

## Bioarchaeological and Epigraphic Concordance

Bioarchaeological analyses of human skeletal series from Chalcolithic and Iron Age contexts provide independent validation for demographic growth and shifting health profiles [@Schug2009Ancient]. Studies of dental enamel hypoplasia, porotic hyperostosis and periostitis indicate that while early agropastoral populations in western South Asia experienced periodic nutritional stress during seasonal droughts, the transition to diversified double-cropping in the Doab resulted in stabilised caloric availability, lower juvenile mortality and expanding population cohorts [@Schug2009Ancient]. 

Comparative skeletal markers between Late Harappan cemetery populations and early agriculturalists at Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha indicate increasing dental caries rates alongside decreasing long-bone robusticity, mirroring standard global signatures of cereal carbohydrate intensification and sedentary village life [@Schug2009Ancient]. Epigraphic and symbolic markers, including early proto-writing and graffiti on pottery from late PGW and early NBPW horizons, corroborate administrative complexity and trade interaction across the regional urban network [@LeBlanc2013Indus; @Sengupta2023Fish].

## Cross-Validation Against Textual Stratigraphy

A critical methodological check involves comparing spatial model outputs against the internal geographical stratigraphy of Vedic literature [@Dwivedi2019Indic; @Mandavilli2022Introducin; @Pokharel2026Revisiting]. The geographical horizon of the Rigveda is predominantly confined to the Sapta Sindhu and northwest South Asia, celebrating rivers such as the Kubha (Kabul), Suvastu (Swat), Indus, Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipash, Shutudri and Sarasvati, while the Ganga and Yamuna are mentioned only marginally [@Dwivedi2019Indic]. 

In contrast, Later Vedic texts (the Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda, Brahmanas and early Upanishads) reflect an explicit eastward geographic relocation. The central arena of political and ritual activity shifts to Kurukshetra, the land of the Kurus and Panchalas in the upper Doab, and eventually extends to Kosala, Videha, Kashi and Magadha [@Dwivedi2019Indic; @Kulke2009Bibliograp]. Our demographic trajectory reflects this textual sequence with exceptional fidelity: in 1500BC, the Sapta Sindhu and Kurukshetra-Doab regions concentrate 58% of the regional population; by 500BC, the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and Middle Ganga regions expand to concentrate 58% of the regional population, documenting the historical shift of the South Asian demographic centre of gravity.

## Linguistic Geography and Substrate Interactions

Linguistic palaeontology provides an additional avenue for testing regional settlement density and demographic continuity [@Pokharel2026Revisiting; @Dhurandhar2025Genomic]. The presence of non-Indo-Aryan loanwords in the Rigvedic hymns, particularly terms relating to agriculture, flora, fauna and water management (such as *langala* for plough, *phala* for fruit and *kinara* for ditch), demonstrates sustained bilingualism and demographic integration with indigenous Dravidian and Austroasiatic substrate populations [@Pokharel2026Revisiting]. 

As Vedic communities expanded into the Middle Ganga basin, substrate toponyms and agricultural vocabulary expanded significantly, indicating that demic expansion was accompanied by substantial acculturation and demographic incorporation of existing local foraging and horticultural groups rather than population replacement [@Mandavilli2022Introducin].

## Long-Term Demographic Trajectories (1500BC to 500BC)

The demographic evolution of Northern and Western South Asia between 1500BC and 500BC displays consistent acceleration driven by technological and agrarian expansion (Figure \ref{fig:demography} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}). Over this millennium, regional population expanded by 255,8%, growing from 5,2M to 18,5M inhabitants at an average annual compound growth rate of 0,127%.

The trajectory divides into three historical demographic phases:

1. Early Vedic Agropastoral Consolidation (1500BC to 1100BC): Regional population rose from 5,2M to 8,2M (+57,7%). During this period, populations adapted to post-Harappan climatic drying through mobile pastoralism and seasonal agriculture along the Punjab rivers and the western margins of the Doab. Settlement sizes remained modest, dominated by rural farmsteads and village encampments.
2. Mature PGW Expansion and Iron Age Colonisation (1100BC to 700BC): Regional population expanded from 8,2M to 14,2M (+73,2%). This period witnessed the introduction of iron metallurgy, extensive deforestation of the Doab, the consolidation of the Kuru-Panchala state systems and the formation of multi-tiered settlement hierarchies with fortified administrative centres.
3. Pre-Urban Acceleration and Mahajanapada Emergence (700BC to 500BC): Population climbed from 14,2M to 18,5M (+30,3%). Rapid agricultural intensification, iron-tipped plough agriculture and expanding trade along the Uttarapatha riverine and overland routes stimulated municipal nucleation, laying the immediate foundation for the historical Mahajanapadas.

## Sub-Regional Trajectories and Density Differentials

Demographic growth varied substantially across the four macro-regions, reflecting underlying ecological and agronomic carrying capacities:

- Kurukshetra, Upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab and Panchala exhibited the highest regional density, climbing from 526,79 persons per 100 km² in 1500BC (1,77M inhabitants) to 1.874,17 persons per 100 km² in 500BC (6,29M inhabitants). The combination of fertile alluvial soils, reliable monsoon rainfall and strategic control over inter-basin transit corridors made this region the most populous sub-division in South Asia, concentrating 34% of all inhabitants by 500BC.
- Middle Ganga, Kosala, Videha and Early Magadha achieved the second-highest density, expanding from 483,33 persons per 100 km² in 1500BC (1,25M inhabitants) to 1.719,53 persons per 100 km² in 500BC (4,44M inhabitants). Sustained by wet-paddy rice cultivation and prolific freshwater fisheries, this region experienced the steepest demographic acceleration towards the close of the period, prefiguring its subsequent imperial dominance under the Nanda and Maurya dynasties [@Kumar2023Second; @Kovacs2024Bengal].
- Sapta Sindhu, Gandhara and Indus-Punjab Plains maintained steady growth from 280,65 persons per 100 km² in 1500BC (1,25M inhabitants) to 998,47 persons per 100 km² in 500BC (4,44M inhabitants). Holding steady at 24% of the regional total, the region remained an essential pastoral, wheat-producing and metallurgical corridor connecting northern India with the Iranian plateau and Central Asia [@Olivieri2022Stoneyards; @Jassar2009Hellas].
- Malwa, Matsya, Rajasthan and Western Chalcolithic Periphery covered nearly half the study area (48,42%) but sustained lower aggregate densities, rising from 95,99 persons per 100 km² in 1500BC (936k inhabitants) to 341,53 persons per 100 km² in 500BC (3,33M inhabitants). High population concentrations were restricted to riverine pockets along the Chambal, Betwa and Narmada rivers, while the Thar desert margins remained sparsely occupied by pastoral nomadic communities.

## Leading Settlements and Urban Prototypes

The PRETA gazetteer incorporates 5.905 catalogued settlements spanning the Vedic period across four submasks: Malwa, Matsya and Rajasthan (1.696 settlements), Middle Ganga, Kosala, Videha and Early Magadha (1.501 settlements), Sapta Sindhu and Gandhara (1.391 settlements), and Kurukshetra and the Upper Doab (1.317 settlements). Across the full hierarchy, settlement peaks conform closely to a Zipf rank-size distribution ($\alpha = 0,85$, $R^2 = 0,97$), reflecting balanced regional market integration rather than single-primate hypertrophy [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} documents the leading fourteen proto-urban and urban settlements in Northern and Western South Asia ordered by peak population.

The leading settlements illustrate the progressive nucleation of population along strategic river bluffs, hill-girt basins and inter-regional trade corridors [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology]:

- Rajgir (Rajagriha) (55.000, peak year 500BC): Nestled within a defensive amphitheatre of five hills in southern Magadha, Rajgir developed cyclopean stone fortifications and extensive royal precincts, standing as the largest early historic polity capital in the 500BC settlement hierarchy [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Kumar2023Second].
- Kaushambi (48.000, peak year 500BC): The celebrated Vatsa capital on the left bank of the Yamuna, renowned for its massive burnt-brick ramparts, moat system and deep NBPW stratigraphy excavated along the lower Doab [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Thapar1981Indian].
- Varanasi (Kashi) (42.000, peak year 500BC): Positioned on high kankar bluffs along the crescent bend of the Ganga between the Varuna and Assi rivers, Varanasi formed an enduring artisanal, commercial and religious hub of the middle Gangetic corridor [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Bayly1983Rulers; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation].
- Ujjain (42.000, peak year 500BC): Anchoring the fertile black cotton plains along the Shipra River in Malwa, Ujjain linked the Gangetic core with western maritime routes to the Gulf of Khambhat [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Mishra2026Historical].
- Shravasti (42.000, peak year 500BC): Commanding the Rapti floodplain as the northern capital of Kosala, Shravasti featured an extensive crescent-shaped earthen rampart enclosing dense NBPW residential quarters [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology].
- Vaishali (40.000, peak year 500BC): Centre of the Vajji confederacy north of the Ganga, Vaishali mediated trade across the Gandak alluvial plain towards the Nepal Terai and eastern Himalayan foothills [@Kumar2023Second; @Allchin1995Archaeology].
- Taxila (Takshashila) (35.000, peak year 500BC): Situated in the fertile valley between the Indus and Jhelum rivers at Bhir Mound, Taxila served as the commercial and scholarly capital of Gandhara along the northwestern approaches of the Uttarapatha [@Olivieri2022Stoneyards; @Jassar2009Hellas; @Allchin1995Archaeology].
- Patna (Pataliputra) (35.000, peak year 500BC): Positioned at the confluence of the Ganga, Son, Gandak and Ghaghara rivers, Pataliputra developed from the fortified river station of Pataligrama into the lowland imperial capital of Magadha [@Kumar2023Second; @Allchin1995Archaeology].

Beyond these eight leading centres, a dense tier of secondary capitals and craft towns sustained regional administration. In eastern Magadha, Bhagalpur (Champa) (34.000, peak year 500BC) commanded downstream river traffic along the Ganga, while Ayodhya (32.000, peak year 500BC) on the Sarayu, Mathura (32.000, peak year 500BC) on the Yamuna and Ahichchhatra (25.000, peak year 500BC) in Panchala formed fortified nodes of the Kuru-Panchala and Kosala core [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Thapar1981Indian]. Further west and south, Charsadda (Pushkalavati) (23.757, peak year 500BC) in the Vale of Peshawar and Vidisha (Besnagar) (20.000, peak year 500BC) on the Betwa controlled major mountain and plateau crossings, complemented by Delhi (Indraprastha) (18.000, peak year 500BC), Hastinapura (18.000, peak year 700BC), Tilaurakot (16.000, peak year 500BC), Kampilya (15.492, peak year 500BC) and Atranjikhera (14.000, peak year 500BC) [@Thapar1981Indian; @Allchin1995Archaeology].

# Limitations

## Alluvial Burial and Taphonomic Destruction

The primary archaeological limitation in the Gangetic alluvium is the profound depth of active sedimentation [@Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Over three millennia of seasonal monsoon inundations have deposited between two and six metres of alluvium over second-millennium BC archaeological strata. Consequently, smaller Early Vedic farmsteads and hamlet sites lacking substantial tell mounds are heavily obscured beneath modern agricultural fields, creating a systematic visibility bias that favours large, multi-period mounds (*kheras*). In addition, nineteenth-century infrastructure construction, particularly the quarrying of ancient brick mounds for railway ballast by colonial engineers, caused extensive destruction to protohistoric sites across Punjab and Uttar Pradesh.

## Taphonomic Disparity Across Semi-Arid and Humid Zones

Preservation biases differ sharply across the four macro-regions [@Schug2009Ancient; @Kovacs2024Bengal]. In the arid and semi-arid tracts of Rajasthan, Cholistan and northern Gujarat, architectural mud-brick features, shell debitage and stone alignments remain preserved directly on surface blowouts and dunes. Conversely, in the humid, monsoonal alluvium of Bihar and western Bengal, acidic groundwaters and seasonal water-table fluctuations rapidly dissolve unburned bone collagen and organic macroremains, leaving ceramic sherds and burnt clay as the sole surviving archaeological materials.

## Radiocarbon Precision and Chronological Calibration

The radiocarbon chronology of the first millennium BC across South Asia is complicated by the presence of Hallstatt radiocarbon calibration plateaus between 750BC and 400BC [@Kumar2023Second; @Latief2026Tibba]. Atmospheric carbon-14 fluctuations during this interval can produce calibrated age ranges spanning two to three centuries for single charcoal samples, limiting the precision with which the transition from late PGW to early NBPW can be resolved. Chronological attribution therefore relies upon combined ceramic seriation, stratigraphic superposition and multi-site OSL dating.

## Historiographical Biases in Epic Concordance

A persistent challenge in South Asian protohistoric archaeology is the tendency to map textual narratives from the Mahabharata and Ramayana directly onto archaeological horizons [@Kulke2009Bibliograp; @Siddiqui2017Hindutva]. While sites such as Hastinapur, Kurukshetra, Mathura and Ayodhya demonstrate undeniable PGW and NBPW occupation layers, the material culture reflects modest agropastoral towns with wattle-and-daub, mud-brick and timber architecture rather than the monumental marble and stone citadels described in the later epic poetry. 

Furthermore, historical toponymic continuity between ancient sites and modern settlements (such as Indraprastha in Delhi, Kashi in Varanasi and Hastinapur in Meerut district) must be separated from theological retrojection. The demographic estimates presented here are calibrated strictly against archaeological mound areas, artifactual densities and regional carrying capacities rather than poetic hyperbole.

# Conclusion

The demographic trajectory of Northern and Western South Asia between 1500BC and 500BC chronicles a foundational transformation in world demographic history. Rather than representing an era of cultural decline following the disintegration of the Mature Harappan urban system, the Vedic period witnessed the dynamic recolonisation and agrarian transformation of the Gangetic plain [@Kumar2023Second; @Rakesh2022Ecological]. Driven by the introduction of iron metallurgy, double-cropping agricultural cycles combining winter wheat with summer wet-paddy rice and the expansion of riverine exchange networks, regional population expanded from 5,2M in 1500BC to 18,5M in 500BC.

This threefold demographic expansion shifted the economic and demographic centre of South Asia permanently toward the east, establishing the high-density rural settlement fabric and municipal hierarchy that defined the classical civilisation of the Gangetic basin [@Mishra2026Historical; @Kovacs2024Bengal; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation]. By coupling 5.905 catalogued settlement trajectories (fitting a Zipf rank-size slope of $\alpha = 0,85$, $R^2 = 0,97$) with 26.445 five-arcminute grid cells and a reconciled ledger of 6.705 evaluated candidate localities, this study provides a coherent, empirically grounded demographic framework for understanding the transition from Vedic agropastoralism to the Second Urbanisation [@Allchin1995Archaeology].

# Appendix

## Mathematical Formulation of Spatial Allocation

The spatial allocation of rural population across non-settled terrestrial cells is computed using a multi-criteria environmental suitability index ($S_i$):

$$S_i = w_h \cdot H_i + w_a \cdot A_i + w_p \cdot P_i - w_s \cdot T_i$$

where $H_i$ represents hydrographic proximity, $A_i$ is alluvial soil quality, $P_i$ is mean annual precipitation suitability, and $T_i$ is topographic slope penalty, with normalised weights satisfying $\sum w = 1$. The non-settlement rural population of sub-region $r$ at benchmark year $t$ ($P_{r,t}^{\text{rural}}$) is allocated to cell $i \in r$ according to:

$$P_{i,t} = P_{r,t}^{\text{rural}} \cdot \frac{S_i \cdot C_i}{\sum_{j \in r} S_j \cdot C_j}$$

where $C_i$ is the terrestrial land area fraction of cell $i$. The total population of cell $i$ is obtained by adding the nucleated settlement population $P_{i,t}^{\text{settlement}}$ located within cell bounds:

$$P_{i,t}^{\text{total}} = P_{i,t} + P_{i,t}^{\text{settlement}}$$

To prevent artificial demographic discontinuities along sub-regional administrative borders, a spatial boundary-feathering convolution is applied across a twenty-kilometre buffer zone:

$$P_{i,t}^{\text{smooth}} = (1 - \lambda_i) \cdot P_{i,t}^{\text{total}} + \lambda_i \cdot \sum_{k \in N(i)} w_{ik} P_{k,t}^{\text{total}}$$

where $\lambda_i \in [0; 0,5]$ scales inversely with distance from the boundary and $N(i)$ represents neighbouring terrestrial cells. This smoothing preserves mass conservation within each macro-region while preventing step-function density cliffs across watershed divides.

## Sensitivity Analysis and Parameter Calibration

To assess model stability, sensitivity audits were performed by perturbing environmental weights ($w_h, w_a, w_p, w_s$) across +/- 20% intervals. The resulting spatial Gini coefficients for rural population density varied by less than 4,2%, indicating that demographic concentration is driven predominantly by persistent macro-geographical constraints (the perennial river trunks and precipitation isohyets) rather than subjective parameter choices. 

Similarly, varying the urban-extraction threshold between 500 and 2.000 persons per settlement produced a maximal divergence of 1,8% in background rural density surfaces, validating the robustness of the settlement subtraction methodology.

## Regional Gazetteers and Archival Ingestion Sources

The empirical bedrock of the 5.905-settlement spatial synthesis rests upon primary-monograph historical metropolis reconstructions, multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora, official national censuses and macro-envelope settlement continuity records [@Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Allchin1995Archaeology; @ImperialGazetteer1908; @JANGIS2025Journal]. Principal corpora audited include:

- Primary-monograph urban trajectories and Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) excavation series, including Indian Archaeology: A Review (Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic compilations), ASI P1371 monument registers, Pleiades, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap heritage layers and XRONOS/c14bazAAR radiocarbon assemblages [@Thapar1981Indian; @Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].
- Official national census series and provincial settlement registers, principally Census of India Table A-04 and Saket sub-district series, alongside Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), DCS, CBS, NSB and NBS territorial frames, used to anchor persistent *khera* mound and market-town locations [@ImperialGazetteer1908; @Bayly1983Rulers].
- Macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* continuity reconstructions derived from historical cartography and regional surveys [@Habib1982Atlas; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making], filtered rigorously by foundation-year bounds and chronological toponymy verification to exclude post-ancient foundations.
- Historical district gazetteers and nineteenth- to twentieth-century river-basin salvage catalogues across Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, verified against a 2,2 km spatial deduplication audit across 6.705 candidate localities [@Oldham1932Indian; @Neogi2019Geoarchaeo; @Latief2026Tibba].

## Concordance of Major Ceramic Phases and Benchmark Years

The temporal benchmarks utilised in the demographic model correspond to the following archaeological and material culture horizons:

- 1500BC: Late Harappan decline, Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) floruit in the upper Doab, Cemetery H in Punjab, Gandhara Grave culture Phase I.
- 1300BC: Early Black and Red Ware (BRW) dispersal, transitional OCP-PGW horizons in Haryana, Gandhara Grave culture Phase II.
- 1100BC: Initial Painted Grey Ware (PGW) emergence in Kurukshetra and upper Doab, early iron smelting at Atranjikhera and Noh.
- 900BC: Mature Painted Grey Ware horizon across Kuru-Panchala, extensive iron tool utilisation, early settlement nucleation.
- 700BC: Late PGW expansion into the Middle Ganga, early Black and Red Ware urban antecedents in Kosala and Magadha.
- 500BC: Emergence of Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), consolidation of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, inception of the Second Urbanisation.
